title: Stash coherence and spillpath investigation (wip)
content:
Status: exploratory notes and repro traces

Summary:
This doc captures an investigation into a recurring tail-latency phenomenon we've observed under mixed chat workloads: short seqlen inference bursts cause repeated KV entries to be ejected to the spillpath (NVMe) and then re-fetched shortly after, amplifying NVMe read traffic and causing p95/p99 response spikes. We call the symptom set "stash coherence" — a pattern where bank-local eviction + remote re-insertion produces churn across the spillpath rather than steady residency.

Why this matters:
- NVMe read amplification = cost + unpredictability; increases unit cost by ~2x in worst cases.
- p99 tail increases (4x in measured traces) during hot-key surges, breaking latency SLOs.
- Causes backpressure into serving runtime (IO threads and memory channel saturation).

Hypothesis (working):
1) Hot windows are concentrated on a small hotset that is bank-skewed (bank 2 & 3).
2) The current eviction policy evicts by global LRU-ish hotness but does not respect bank-local residency capacity, so entries get pushed back and forth across banks.
3) Reinsertions for the same key frequently miss the local bank and cause remote fetch + NVMe read (if the page was already spilled), creating a "spill->re-fetch->evict->spill" cycle (amplified by prefetch backoff logic).
4) Memory channel bandwidth becomes the choke; when one channel saturates, eviction jitter increases and increases the chance of repeated NVMe ops.

Environment / testbed:
- Model: rw-13B-quant (production-ish).
- Node type: 8xA100-80GB-equivalent with 6 memory channels (synthetic mapping).
- OS / NVMe: Ubuntu 22.04, NVMe SSD (PCIe4) sustained 6.4 GB/s write, 15 GB/s read burst.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime v0.72.1 + local perf hooks.
- Workload: mix of 80% short prompts (avg seqlen 32) and 20% long contexts (avg seqlen 1024) with client-side hot-key skew (Zipf alpha 1.2).

What we measured (representative run):
- Baseline (no hot skew): NVMe read QPS 18k, avg read throughput 3.2 GB/s, p99 latency 22 ms.
- Hot skew run: NVMe read QPS 42k, avg read throughput 7.1 GB/s, p99 latency 86 ms.
- Read amplification: measured logical page read count / unique page request = 2.1x under hot skew.
- Memory channel utilization (perf samples): channel 2 = 94% busy, channel 5 = 41% busy.
- Eviction churn metric (new telemetry): per-minute evictions jumped from 1200 -> 7600.

Traces / signals we collected:
- Kernel iostat / blktrace snippets: repeated small (4–16 KB) tail reads clustered every 12–18 ms during surges.
- Serving runtime logs (KV debug): sequence showing key X evicted at t=1.203s from bank-id=2, fetched from NVMe at t=1.215s, reinserted into bank-id=4, evicted again at t=1.230s — pattern repeats for same key.
- Per-bank residency counters (instrumented): bank 2 resident ratio drifted 12% -> 47% while global free pages stayed constant.
- Flamegraph (CPU): IO thread spikes coincide with re-insert code path and async completion handler.

Quick repro steps (local):
1) Start runtime with --kv-bank-count=6 --eviction-hysteresis-ms=8 --local-pinning=false --enable-prefetch=true
2) Run synthetic client: workload/hot-skew-run.py --seed 42 --zipf 1.2 --duration 10m --short-p=0.8 --QPS 2400
3) Capture perf & blktrace for 2m window after warmup.

Notable microbench experiments tried so far:
A) Turned off prefetch: NVMe read QPS dropped 28%, p99 improved to 61 ms. Suggests prefetch interacts badly with bank-skew.
B) Increased eviction-hysteresis from 8ms -> 32ms: reduced eviction churn by 42%, but median latency increased marginally (3-5ms) — tradeoff may be acceptable.
C) Enabled local pinning for top-100 hot keys (client-side hint): NVMe reads for those keys dropped 94%, overall read throughput dropped 18%.
D) Bank-aware admission prototype (brokered): reduced cross-bank insertions by ~37% in synthetic run.

Preliminary root-cause model:
- The eviction policy is globally oblivious to where entries were previously resident. Under skew, a bank that temporarily accepts many inserts will later evict them en masse because global metrics indicate they are hot but local capacity exceeded; other banks reinsert, causing cross-bank migrations.
- Migration + small read granularity on NVMe increases IO amplification. Memory channel hotspots occur because eviction and reinsertion ops concentrate on a subset of banks mapped to physical channels.

Short-term mitigations (cheap, low-risk):
- Increase default eviction-hysteresis to 24–32 ms for production clusters that serve skewed chat workloads. Owner: Leah (PR in progress).
- Disable aggressive prefetch for single-tenant heavy-hotset customers (runtime flag). Owner: Ethan.
- Add a quick runtime knob to cap cross-bank reinsertion rate per second (rate limiter) to prevent thrashing. Owner: Marcus (prototype).

Medium-term engineering work (prioritized):
- Implement per-bank admission control: prefer reinsertion into the original bank if the page was recently resident there (fingerprint-based lookup). Benefit: reduces cross-bank churn. Effort: 2–3 sprints.
- Track per-bank eviction scores and apply hysteresis per-bank instead of global. Should flatten eviction storms. Effort: 1–2 sprints.
- Improve NVMe aggregation: coalesce small page reads into batched async reads when we detect repeat misses for the same logical region to reduce PCIe overhead. Effort: 1 sprint + storage perf tests.

Telemetry & experiments needed (next runs):
- Collect per-key re-fetch histogram (how many times a logical key hits NVMe within 1s). Target: identify top-10 offenders.
- Run A/B with eviction-hysteresis 8/24/48 ms across same traffic and compare p95/p99 and NVMe read amplification.
- Stress test bank-aware admission under mixed multi-tenant load to ensure fairness stable.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Does prefetch predictor itself cause eviction of pages that would otherwise remain resident? (initial evidence: yes, but need controlled test).
- Are there pathological interactions with the thread pool ordering (IO completion callback priority) that amplify eviction reinserts?
- How much of the phenomenon maps to physical NUMA node boundaries vs logical bank mapping? We should run a NUMA-aware variant to isolate.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Marcus: deliver a small-rate-limiter prototype for cross-bank reinserts (due 2025-11-18).
- Leah: open PR to bump default eviction-hysteresis and add metrics (eviction-churn-per-bank) (PR # TODO).
- Aisha: run a 3-day customer-sim cohort with prefetch toggled off and collect cost delta.
- Ethan: instrument key-level re-fetch histograms and add to dashboard (confluence chart).

Notes to self / brain-dumps:
- Hot-key pinning works but is a brittle workaround for multi-tenant clusters — needs eviction-aware contract with tenant-level quotas.
- Consider "soft residency" where we mark a page as recently-fetched and bias insertions to stay in same bank for N ms. This is cheaper than full fingerprint lookup.

References:
- Linked artifacts at top (Jira INF-2419 describes customer case).
- Perf capture: s3://perf-dumps/2025-11-04/stash-coherence-run-42.tar.gz

Conclusion (current verdict):
We believe stash coherence is a real amplification loop caused by cross-bank reinserts combined with prefetch and small NVMe read granularity. Short-term mitigations (increase hysteresis, disable prefetch) reduce the immediate pain. Longer-term fixes should be bank-aware admission + smarter NVMe aggregation. Next milestone: prototype rate-limiter + re-fetch histograms and run A/B by 2025-11-18.

-- Marcus
